existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: The middle ground: accommodation through mutual invention and creative misunderstanding between Algonquian villages and empires in the Great Lakes region, 1650–1815 (1991)
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: White's own statement, The Middle Ground (1991). Introduction, p. ix (Cambridge Core first-page excerpt: the full page, folio observed): histories of Indian–white relations have had 'but two outcomes', stories 'of conquest and assimilation' or 'of cultural persistence'; their tellers 'miss a larger process and a larger truth. The meeting of sea and continent, like the meeting of whites and Indians, creates as well as destroys.' The next page (1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi; witnessed only by Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 edition, page images not seen, the 1991 page inferred) defines the middle ground, in paraphrase, as the space between cultures, between peoples, and between empires and the stateless world of villages, where differences were accommodated through creative and often expedient misunderstanding, and explains it by the long periods in which whites could neither command Indians nor ignore them. Chapter 2 opening (p. 50, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt, folio observed): French and Algonquians 'had to arrive at some common conception of suitable ways of acting; they had to create what I have already referred to as a middle ground. The creation of the middle ground involved a process of mutual invention by both the French and the Algonquians.' It rested on 'the need of people to find a means, other than force, to gain the cooperation or consent of foreigners' (p. 52), and was, in paraphrase, a product both of everyday life and of formal diplomacy between distinct peoples (p. 53) (both Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 edition; page numbers as the snippet results give them, taken to match 1991). Chapter 3 opening (p. 94, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt): the fur trade was 'a constantly changing compromise, a conduit, between two local models of the exchange'. Epilogue (p. 518, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt): 'The compromises intrinsic in the middle ground yielded to stark choices between assimilation and otherness.' In-period reception, each read in full. Savard (1992; Université de Montréal anthropologist) judges the book's circularity 'inattaquable' and suited to 'bien d'autres époques et régions de l'Amérique du Nord', but asks whether the Algonquians' shattered prior state and Iroquois military supremacy, 'cet autre mythe fondateur de la république américaine', were needed to explain it (p. 120). Edmunds (1993) calls the thesis 'a valuable model for the exploration of the Indian-French relationship' (p. 148) and the book possibly 'a landmark volume in the ethnohistory of the Great Lakes tribes', but finds 'his arguments for the period after 1770 are less convincing' (p. 149). D. R. Miller (1994, Canadian Journal of Native Studies, from the Saskatchewan Indian Federated College) calls it 'an extraordinary benchmark in the scholarship of European and Aboriginal relations' (p. 157), notes that White 'deemphasizes the specificity of a small number of groups in the larger Great Lakes region that are neither Iroquoian or Algonquian' (p. 158), and writes that 'The challenge for a similar study with emphasis upon the north side of the Great Lakes is obvious' (p. 170). The edge records a scholar's interpretation of Indigenous–imperial relations, which the Indigenous history entry lists as related scholarship; it does not make the work an Indigenous historical practice or a source of Indigenous authority. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: White's 2011 preface (Google Books search-within snippets only) answers Merrell's in-period critique (Into the American Woods, 1999; cited pp. xx–xxi) and the later critiques of Havard (Empire et métissages, 2003; p. xvi) and Deloria ('What Is the Middle Ground, Anyway?', 2006; cited p. xii; both unread here): the middle ground 'did not involve the achievement of a widespread mutual understanding and appreciation between Europeans and Indian peoples. People did not come together to love one another' (p. xxi), and he did not think that 'every time you find this process at work you would find the construction of a coherent space that is the equivalent of pays d'en haut' (p. xiii). McNeill (2003; text-layer PDF) reports that the concept 'struck historians of Japan and medieval Austria as useful for their own studies' (p. 37).

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Environmental change through land use, subsistence and labour: Island County (1980), the roots of Native dependency (1983) and the Columbia as an organic machine (1995), with an early survey of the field (1985)
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: White's own statements, known for his books only through Google Books search-within snippets (page images not seen) and therefore paraphrased where the wording carries the claim. Land Use, Environment, and Social Change (1980; snippets of the 1992 paperback, whose body text is the 1980 text; p. 7 as given in the snippet results): White presents the book as departing somewhat from recent environmental history, which he describes as mostly a variant of intellectual and political history, by tracing the environmental impact of Indian and later intruding peoples and its consequences for their societies; on the same page he credits James Malin's Great Plains studies, ignored by most historians, as a trail to follow. In the preface to the 1992 edition (November 1991; snippet, folio xviii inferred from Google Books page ids that carry the printed folios xi, xvi and xvii) he judges his own use of ecology: 'I used ecological concepts like community, succession, climax, and ecosystem unproblematically even though within the discipline of ecology those ideas had already come under attack'. Cronon's foreword (October 1991; snippets, folio xi observed) places the book among White's contributions 'to environmental history, to the history of the American West, to Indian history, and to American history generally' and calls it 'a textbook case of an underappreciated classic' (p. xi). The Organic Machine (1995; snippets of the preface, whose printed folios were not visible, and of the conclusion, p. 112 taken from the Google Books page id, not seen as a printed folio), in paraphrase: White examines the Columbia as an organic machine, an energy system modified by human intervention that keeps natural, unmade qualities; human labour is energy as much as the river's flow or the calories salmon store for their journey; environmentalists, he argues, distance humans from nature by favouring the eye over the hand and contemplation over work; and the conclusion finds the nature in us in our labour and energy (p. 112). In-period third-party readings: Cronon (1993; OCR of the author-hosted page scan) footnotes Land Use and The Roots of Dependency (nn. 15, 23) for the lesson that 'the horse was not simply a European invader, but a complex cultural entity' (p. 9); D. R. Miller (1994; PDF read in full) calls him 'The social and environmental historian Richard White' (p. 157) and quotes The Middle Ground that dependency 'is an economic, political, and social relationship, but can also be an environmental relationship' (p. 169). On the 1985 survey (unread; paywalled): Worster (1990, read in the 2002–03 Portuguese translation, n. 5, p. 42) calls it the best effort to trace the field's emergence, 'pelo menos em uma parte influente do mundo', reporting White's view that frontier and western history was the formative influence; Cronon's 1994 graduate syllabus assigns it 'read for main themes' (p. 4); in Canada, Cook (1990) cites it (n. 4) for Turner and Webb as 'important, if declining, influences into the 1950s' (p. 6). A contribution, not a founding. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: Isenberg (2013) names White among historians who 'synthesized the material and cultural approaches to the environment' (p. 87) and quotes his 1990 round-table objection that Worster's scheme reduced culture to 'superstructure in the old vulgar Marxist sense' (pp. 88–89, citing JAH 76, pp. 1112–1113; the JAH text is unread).

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Examines railroad construction, finance, freight markets and recurrent bankruptcy as problems of economic history, connecting private returns with public subsidies (Railroaded, 2011)
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: White’s own selected 2011 interview passages distinguish profits from construction and financing from the operation of railroads, and examine political favours and bankruptcy. This records an inquiry into economic organization and corporate capitalism, not founding a field, accepted agreement with other named historians or an influence inferred from bibliographies. The complete book is unread.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: White reads Turner’s settlement story alongside Buffalo Bill’s conquest story as complementary frontier myths that marginalize Indigenous dispossession (1994).
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Selected White transcription corroborated by Richard W. Steele’s complete 1995 scholarly review. Exact book pagination and illustrations uncollated; the full chapter remains unread. This is White’s interpretation of Turner, not independent validation of every exhibition object.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Calloway draws on White’s account of negotiated Native power and cultural accommodation to unsettle an English-centered, east-to-west account of early America.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Own 2011 interview explains the particular resource; Parmenter 1999 p124 separately identifies White alongside James Axtell and James Merrell in New Worlds for All. Their credit remains plural. Bailyn 1995 also names White’s resource in Calloway’s Revolution book. These are distinct witnesses, consolidated in one contribution claim. The complete books and Calloway’s 1992 review remain unread.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: DuVal: in the Arkansas Valley Native peoples dominated and incorporated colonists; 'only relatively weak people desired the kind of compromises inherent in a middle ground' (2006)
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: This arrow represents Kathleen DuVal's argument (The Native Ground, 2006), not a verdict of the field. Introduction unread; the central sentence, p. 5, is witnessed identically by two readers read here: Piker (AHR 112:3, 2007, extract read) and Isaac (ActiveHistory, 2021, read in full). Piker also quotes p. 5: colonialism 'met neither accommodation nor resistance but incorporation'. Hatfield (Common-Place 7:2, 2007, read in full): DuVal 'argues that unlike the peoples of the Great Lakes region Richard White studies … Arkansas Indians dominated their region well into the nineteenth century … because they were not a population of refugees as were the Indians in the Great Lakes'. White's side, in his own words: a middle ground needs 'a rough balance of power, mutual need … and an inability by either side to commandeer enough force to compel the other to change' (2006, p. 10, as quoted in English by Avila 2011, p. 272). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.4)

existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: This arrow represents Pekka Hämäläinen's book as read by Thomas Grillot (Books & Ideas, 20 January 2014, read in full): 'There is little or no middle ground for compromise between Indians and non-Indians in his book (p. 130): the Comanches are too powerful for this'; Grillot also judges that 'the criticism of the concept of the middle ground … seems here to have been pushed too far'. The book itself is unread. White's own reading of it, 2011 preface p. xv (Google Books snippet, source pe131_richard_white_middle_ground_preface_2011): 'no middle ground emerges'. Grillot records that White signed the preface to the French translation. White's side, in his own words: a middle ground needs 'a rough balance of power, mutual need … and an inability by either side to commandeer enough force to compel the other to change' (2006, p. 10, as quoted in English by Avila 2011, p. 272). existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Witgen: in a Native New World the French moved, as Reda puts it, from misunderstanding to being 'essentially delusional' about their relations; European possession of the interior 'never occurred' (2012)
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: This arrow represents Michael Witgen's book as read by John Reda (H-AmIndian, July 2014, read in full), p. 2: 'Up to this point, Witgen's explanation seems little different from Richard White's middle ground, where cultural misinterpretations often led to workable understandings between Europeans and Native Americans. Witgen, however, pushes further to demonstrate that the French passed quickly from misunderstanding Native Americans to becoming essentially delusional about the nature of their relationships with them.' Witgen as quoted by Reda: 'the possession of large portions of Native North America by the empires of Europe never occurred' (p. 28); the British 'simply inherited the illusion of empire' (p. 217). 'Delusional' is Reda's word, not Witgen's. The book is unread. White's side, in his own words: a middle ground needs 'a rough balance of power, mutual need … and an inability by either side to commandeer enough force to compel the other to change' (2006, p. 10, as quoted in English by Avila 2011, p. 272). (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.6)

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: White in 2021 (interview published in Portuguese translation): the more anthropology he read, the more critical he became of ethnohistory as a hybrid, and he is increasingly wary of upstreaming; the New Indian History now looks primitive, and its agency argument could go too far
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Paraphrase only. Fontella, História (São Paulo) 41 (2022), e2022054 (read in full): White's English answers, received 30 April 2021, are published only in Fontella's Portuguese translation, so no English words are attributed to him. p. 10: 'quanto mais Antropologia eu lia, mais crítico eu me tornava do híbrido: Etnohistória'; 'A New Indian History parece bastante primitiva agora … a tendência poderia ir longe demais, disfarçando as enormes forças que muitas vezes matavam muitos deles e destruíam suas sociedades'; p. 15: 'estou cada vez mais desconfiado do upstreaming'; p. 16: upstreaming assumes that a belief, ritual or practice 'contém um significado inato que não muda significativamente à medida que viaja no tempo'. The later worry about agency is his own; it is not evidence about Brownlie and Kelm's 1994 essay. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.1)

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: White challenges Wiebe’s portrayal of a weak laissez-faire state by emphasizing government intervention, delegated power and corruption.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Own answer in2017Stanford interview names both Hofstadter and Wiebe, then specifies tariffs, subsidies and social welfare alongside limited administrative capacity. Collective criticism retains both targets; dossier only proposes the assigned Wiebe pair. White’s account is attributed and not turned into a claim that Wiebe ignored every state action. Tyrrell2018p401 similarly qualifies Wiebe’s weak-state model but is a distinct critic; no full White or Wiebe monograph claimed read.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Wood contrasts White’s account of pre-Revolutionary Algonquian accommodation with Taylor’s post-Revolutionary Iroquois separation.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Explicit Wood2006mediation109 compares titles and arguments across different regions/periods. Undirected comparison, not evidence of an identical historical test, personal transmission or wholesale Taylor rejection of White. Full original books unread.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Foner questions whether White’s Greater Reconstruction framework homogenizes federal action in the South and West,and argues that its emphasis on defeat and violence gives too little attention to Black political leaders.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Own 2018 review P17–18 distinguishes protecting freedpeople’s rights against southern elites from dispossessing western Native peoples. P12–16/19–22 praises White’s synthesis, economic explanations and breadth. This is a particular argument/coverage criticism with positive appraisal, not proof every national comparison is invalid. Foner’s reported index omissions not independently collated; White’s complete book unread. Richard White differs from Ronald C. White and Chernow reviewed alongside.
